# Architecture and training objective {#app:objective}

This appendix states the policy architecture and optimization objective used in the reported experiments. The purpose is to separate three implementation facts that matter for interpretation: what every policy observes, how learned messages enter the PPO update, and which architectural differences remain between learned and externally generated message-source controls.

## Observation and network architecture

For agent $i$ at round $t$, the full-history observation used by the action policy is
$$
o_{i,t}
=
\bigl[
\hat f_{i,t},
\; e_i,
\; c_{t-1},
\; a_{i,t-1},
\; \mathrm{EWMA}_t,
\; \mathrm{onehot}(m_{1,t}),
\dots,
\mathrm{onehot}(m_{S,t})
\bigr],
$$
where $S=4$ is the number of sender slots, $\hat f_{i,t}$ is the noisy private signal, $e_i$ is the endowment, $c_{t-1}$ is the previous-round group cooperation fraction, $a_{i,t-1}$ is the agent's own previous executed action, and $\mathrm{EWMA}_t$ is an exponentially weighted moving average of recent group cooperation. The message block contains one-hot encodings of the token delivered from each sender slot. In \texttt{no-comm}, the message block is absent. In reduced-history runs, the wrapper preserves the same tensor shape but zeros the temporal-history slice $(c_{t-1}, a_{i,t-1}, \mathrm{EWMA}_t)$. In communication-enabled training, message dropout is applied before the received message one-hots are appended.

Each agent has separate feed-forward multilayer perceptrons for the action policy and value function, each with two hidden layers of width 64 and ReLU nonlinearities:
$$
\pi_i(a \mid o_{i,t}) = \mathrm{Cat}\!\bigl(\mathrm{softmax}(f^{(a)}_i(o_{i,t}))\bigr),
\qquad
V_i(\tilde o_{i,t}) = f^{(v)}_i(\tilde o_{i,t}),
$$
where $\mathrm{Cat}$ denotes a categorical distribution. The value network receives the same observation plus a scalar within-episode time feature,
$$
\tilde o_{i,t} = [o_{i,t};\, t/(T-1)].
$$

For learned communication, each sender has a separate message policy of the same MLP form,
$$
\psi_i(m \mid o_{i,t}) = \mathrm{Cat}\!\bigl(\mathrm{softmax}(f^{(m)}_i(o_{i,t}))\bigr),
$$
with vocabulary size $|\mathcal V|=2$. Exogenous source-mode controls are implemented differently: when \texttt{msg\_source\_mode} is \texttt{uniform}, \texttt{public\_random}, \texttt{fixed0}, or \texttt{fixed1}, no trainable sender message actor is instantiated. Messages are generated externally and passed through the same receiver-side observation wrapper. Thus the receiver interface is matched across communication-enabled modes, but only the learned mode trains a sender message policy.

## Returns and PPO objective

Agents are trained independently with generalized advantage estimation (GAE). Let $r_{i,t}$ be the reward after reward scaling, $V_i(\tilde o_{i,t})$ the value prediction, $d_t \in \{0,1\}$ the episode-termination indicator, $\gamma=0.99$ the discount factor, and $\lambda=0.95$ the GAE parameter. The temporal-difference residual and GAE recursion are
$$
\delta_{i,t}
=
r_{i,t}
 + \gamma (1-d_t) V_i(\tilde o_{i,t+1})
 - V_i(\tilde o_{i,t}),
$$
$$
A_{i,t}
=
\delta_{i,t}
 + \gamma \lambda (1-d_t) A_{i,t+1},
\qquad
R_{i,t} = A_{i,t} + V_i(\tilde o_{i,t}).
$$
Advantages are standardized within agent before the PPO update.

For the action policy, with PPO clip parameter $\epsilon=0.2$, the clipped ratio is
$$
r^{(a)}_{i,t}
=
\frac{\pi_i(a_{i,t}\mid o_{i,t})}{\pi_i^{\mathrm{old}}(a_{i,t}\mid o_{i,t})},
$$
and the action surrogate minimized by the optimizer is
$$
\mathcal L^{\mathrm{act}}_{i}
=
-\mathbb E_t
\Bigl[
\min\!\bigl(
r^{(a)}_{i,t} A_{i,t},
\mathrm{clip}(r^{(a)}_{i,t}, 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) A_{i,t}
\bigr)
\Bigr].
$$

For learned senders, the message decision is updated jointly with the action decision. On timesteps where sender $i$ emits message $m_{i,t}$, the implementation forms the joint ratio
$$
r^{(a,m)}_{i,t}
=
\exp\!\Bigl(
\log \pi_i(a_{i,t}\mid o_{i,t})
 + \log \psi_i(m_{i,t}\mid o_{i,t})
 - \log \pi_i^{\mathrm{old}}(a_{i,t}\mid o_{i,t})
 - \log \psi_i^{\mathrm{old}}(m_{i,t}\mid o_{i,t})
\Bigr),
$$
and uses the clipped joint surrogate
$$
\mathcal L^{\mathrm{joint}}_{i}
=
-\mathbb E_t
\Bigl[
\min\!\bigl(
r^{(a,m)}_{i,t} A_{i,t},
\mathrm{clip}(r^{(a,m)}_{i,t}, 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) A_{i,t}
\bigr)
\Bigr].
$$
If a minibatch contains both sender-updated and action-only samples for the same agent, the implementation averages the two surrogates in proportion to the sample counts. In exogenous source-mode controls and in \texttt{no-comm}, the joint message term is absent because no trainable message actor exists.

The value loss is mean squared error,
$$
\mathcal L^{\mathrm{value}}_{i}
=
\mathbb E_t\bigl[(V_i(\tilde o_{i,t}) - R_{i,t})^2\bigr],
$$
and the action and message entropy terms are
$$
\mathcal H^{(a)}_{i,t}
=
H\!\bigl(\pi_i(\cdot \mid o_{i,t})\bigr),
\qquad
\mathcal H^{(m)}_{i,t}
=
H\!\bigl(\psi_i(\cdot \mid o_{i,t})\bigr).
$$

For each agent and minibatch, the optimized loss is
$$
\mathcal L_i
=
\mathcal L^{\mathrm{policy}}_i
 + c_v \mathcal L^{\mathrm{value}}_i
 - \beta_a \, \mathbb E_t[\mathcal H^{(a)}_{i,t}]
 - \beta_m \, \mathbb E_t[\mathcal H^{(m)}_{i,t}],
$$
where $c_v=0.5$, $\mathcal L^{\mathrm{policy}}_i$ is $\mathcal L^{\mathrm{act}}_i$, $\mathcal L^{\mathrm{joint}}_i$, or their count-weighted minibatch average as described above, and the message-entropy term is present only when the agent has a learned message actor. In the reported runs, $\beta_a$ is annealed linearly from $0.01$ to $0.001$ and $\beta_m$ from $0.01$ to $0.0$. The objective contains no positive-signalling or listening auxiliary losses.

## Remaining asymmetries across conditions

Communication-specific auxiliary shaping is not part of the objective. Even so, the arms are not identical optimization problems. Turning communication on adds received-message inputs to the receiver policy, and learned communication additionally adds a trainable sender message head. Exogenous source modes match the receiver-side input interface but replace the sender policy with externally generated messages, so message-source controls should be read as tests of which channel properties are sufficient under the implemented training design, not as tests between fully identical parameterizations.

```{=latex}
  Family & What it tests & What it cannot identify \\
  \midrule
  Base checkpoint suites & Descriptive gap between separately trained comm and no-comm policies & Whether the gap is caused by messages vs.\ broader training-path differences \\
  Direct from-scratch message-source controls & Whether learned senders outperform matched exogenous source types under the same receiver interface and training objective & Which aspect of per-sender variation drives the effect: cross-slot independence, marginal entropy, or interaction with temporal context \\
  Comm $\times$ history factorial & Whether communication's training-time benefit requires temporal observation features & Which specific features mediate the interaction \\
  Frozen-policy interventions & Online dependence of a fixed policy on its message input & Training-time value of the communication channel \\
  Single-slot sender probes & Input sensitivity of a frozen policy to one sender's token & Full equilibrium effects of a sender choosing a message \\
  Within-seed conventions \& transfer & Which message features and transfer tests generalize across seeds & Causal effects of changing message features under matched histories \\
  \bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
```

## Aggregate cancellation and polarity alignment {#app:aggregate-cancellation}

The frozen sender-specific interventions in the main text are interventional endpoint tests. This appendix adds the descriptive complement: natural receiver- and sender-semantics summaries can look weak in the aggregate even when sender-conditioned structure remains strong.

These summaries are observational, not interventional. They condition on message value or sender identity under the natural rollout distribution of the frozen policy; they therefore describe endpoint structure and convention fragmentation, but they do not by themselves identify what would happen under a forced message intervention.

For the diagnostics below, we compare the aggregate any-token effect
$$
  \delta_{\mathrm{agg}}(\fhat_{\mathrm{bin}}) =
  P(C \mid \exists\, k: m_k=1,\fhat_{\mathrm{bin}})
  -
  P(C \mid \forall\, k: m_k=0,\fhat_{\mathrm{bin}})
$$
to the sender-conditioned effect
$$
  \delta_{i \rightarrow j}(\fhat_{\mathrm{bin}}) =
  P(C \mid m_i=1,\fhat_{\mathrm{bin}})
  -
  P(C \mid m_i=0,\fhat_{\mathrm{bin}}).
$$
For sender polarity, we summarize each sender's endpoint convention by
$$
  \Delta_{\mathrm{high-low}} =
  P(m_i=1 \mid \fhat \ge 4.5) - P(m_i=1 \mid \fhat < 1.5),
$$
then ask whether different senders share the same sign or split into opposite polarities.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(
    render_table_here(
        "tbl-alignment",
        r"Aggregate cancellation explains why pooled token statistics understate message dependence. Aggregate any-token effects average $P(C \mid \exists\, k: m_k=1,\fhat_{\mathrm{bin}}) - P(C \mid \forall\, k: m_k=0,\fhat_{\mathrm{bin}})$ over private-signal bins; per-sender effects average $|P(C \mid m_i=1,\fhat_{\mathrm{bin}}) - P(C \mid m_i=0,\fhat_{\mathrm{bin}})|$ over non-self sender--receiver pairs and bins (skipping incomplete sender-token pairs). Regime-sign alignment is the mean pairwise product of sender polarity signs, where polarity is $P(m_i=1 \mid \fhat \ge 4.5) - P(m_i=1 \mid \fhat < 1.5)$; values near $0$ indicate mixed sender polarities. Mean $\pm$ SEM over 15 seeds.",
        render_alignment_table(),
    )
)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
ratio_150 = math_text(f"{fmt_num(semantics_value('150000', 'aggregate_vs_sender_ratio'), 1)}\\times")
print(
    f"At 150k, the aggregate signed observational token effect is essentially zero: {pp_pm_math(semantics_value('150000', 'aggregate_signed_mean'), semantics_value('150000', 'aggregate_signed_sem'))} (Figure \\ref{{fig-alignment}}, Panel A). Yet the corresponding per-sender absolute effect remains {abs_pp_pm_math(semantics_value('150000', 'per_sender_abs_mean'), semantics_value('150000', 'per_sender_abs_sem'))}, about {ratio_150} larger than the aggregate absolute effect. This is aggregate cancellation: sender-conditioned endpoint effects survive, but many point in different directions and largely vanish when pooled."
)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(
    f"Sender polarity diagnostics show why the cancellation persists (Figure \\ref{{fig-alignment}}, Panel B). The mean regime-sign alignment index is only {math_text(fmt_num(semantics_value('50000', 'alignment_regime_mean'), 2))} at 50k and {math_text(fmt_num(semantics_value('150000', 'alignment_regime_mean'), 2))} at 150k, while mixed-polarity seeds account for {int(semantics_value('50000', 'mixed_regime_seed_count'))}/{int(semantics_value('50000', 'n_seeds'))} and {int(semantics_value('150000', 'mixed_regime_seed_count'))}/{int(semantics_value('150000', 'n_seeds'))} seeds respectively. Even at 150k, the mean absolute sender polarity remains {abs_pp_pm_math(semantics_value('150000', 'mean_abs_regime_delta'), semantics_value('150000', 'mean_abs_regime_delta_sem'))}. Different senders within the same trained population therefore often disagree on what token 1 tends to signal, which is better described as sender-indexed dialects than as one shared sign convention."
)
```

## Grouped surrogate specification {#app:lowdim-spec}

The grouped-surrogate analysis in Section \ref{sec-lowdim} is a predictive check rather than a test of causal mechanism. The target is the receiver's binary action on natural frozen traces from the learned communication policy, filtered to \texttt{cond1}, \texttt{ablation=none}, \texttt{history\_intervention=none}, and checkpoint 150k. For each focal multiplier, the fitting set is subsampled to at most 5,000 observations per training seed; grouped 5-fold cross-validation then holds out entire seeds, so each fold tests whether a mapping learned on some trained populations predicts behavior in unseen populations.

All surrogate models use the same pipeline as the analysis code: standardized numeric inputs, one-hot categorical inputs, and a \texttt{liblinear} logistic regression with \texttt{max\_iter=2000}. The models differ only in how the message stream is encoded:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(
    render_table_here(
        "tbl-lowdim-spec",
        r"Exact grouped-surrogate specification for Section \ref{sec-lowdim}. All models predict the receiver's action on natural frozen traces at 150k. Numeric columns are standardized; categorical columns are one-hot encoded. Grouped 5-fold cross-validation holds out entire training seeds. The only change across rows is the message encoding.",
        render_lowdim_spec_table(),
    )
)
```

The full-pattern variable \texttt{pattern} is receiver-indexed: it records which specific senders delivered which bits to that receiver, so it can express sender-specific conventions. Consequently, poor held-out performance of \texttt{history\_pattern} means that these detailed sender-indexed mappings do not transfer cleanly across independently trained seeds, even though they matter strongly within a seed.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(
    render_table_here(
        "tbl-lowdim-surrogate",
        r"What message features generalize across independently trained seeds? Each row is a logistic regression fit on natural 150k frozen traces from some seeds and evaluated on held-out seeds. Numeric inputs are standardized; categorical inputs are one-hot encoded. Models differ only in message encoding: none, any-token, count-of-ones, one bit per sender slot, or a one-hot full received pattern. Entries are mean held-out log loss; lower is better. If sender-specific patterns generalized across seeds, richer sender-aware models would outperform simpler ones on held-out seeds.",
        render_lowdim_surrogate_table(),
    )
)
```

## Cross-seed message transfer {#app:transfer}

```{python}

#| output: asis
print(
    render_table_here(
        "tbl-transfer",
        r"Do learned message conventions transfer across independently trained populations? A trained receiver from one seed is fed messages produced by a different seed's senders, with all weights frozen. Cooperation means are averaged over ordered receiver--donor pairs. The pre-specified row shows the best-performing simple polarity rule (\texttt{weighted\_slot\_sign}); the post hoc pair-specific flip row is an upper bound selected after seeing the outcome. The final row counts how many receiver seeds (out of 15) achieve donor-averaged upper-bound transfer above their own natural baseline.",
        render_cross_seed_transfer_table(),
    )
)
```

This appendix adds the direct behavioral counterpart to the grouped-surrogate analysis in the main text. For each receiver seed, we transplant a donor seed's learned message stream while keeping the receiver policy fixed. The matched transfer suite uses the same evaluation seed for raw foreign identity and the global $0 \leftrightarrow 1$ flip, reports both ordered-pair and receiver-level summaries, and considers only these two possibilities.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(
    render_table_here(
        "tbl-transfer-appendix",
        r"Extended cross-seed transfer results at 150k, showing that foreign message streams provide little benefit beyond random controls. Ordered-pair columns average over receiver--donor pairs; receiver columns average donor means within each receiver seed. The flip-allowed row takes the better of foreign identity and a global $0 \leftrightarrow 1$ flip for each receiver--donor pair (a post hoc upper bound).",
        render_transfer_appendix_table(),
    )
)
```

The post hoc flip-allowed row takes the better of two options after seeing the outcome, inflating the transfer estimate. To test whether the polarity alignment is predictable, we evaluate three simple pre-specified rules that predict noflip or flipall for each receiver--donor pair based on sender polarity diagnostics computed from natural frozen traces (not from the transfer outcomes): \texttt{seed\_mean\_sign} (sign of the seed-level mean polarity), \texttt{majority\_slot\_sign} (majority vote of per-sender polarity signs), and \texttt{weighted\_slot\_sign} (weighted by absolute polarity magnitude). The table below shows \texttt{weighted\_slot\_sign}, which is the best-performing of the three; all three yield qualitatively identical results.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(
    render_table_here(
        "tbl-nonoracle-transfer",
        r"Pre-specified polarity rules fail to recover the post hoc upper bound on cross-seed transfer at 150k. The table shows \texttt{weighted\_slot\_sign}, the best-performing of three simple polarity rules tested (\texttt{seed\_mean\_sign}, \texttt{majority\_slot\_sign}, \texttt{weighted\_slot\_sign}); all three yield qualitatively identical results. Random controls appear below the midrule for comparison. The gap between the predicted-rule and post hoc rows quantifies how much of the apparent transfer is due to pair-specific selection.",
        render_nonoracle_transfer_table(),
    )
)
```

None of the three pre-specified rules recovers the post hoc upper-bound advantage. At $f=3.5$, the best predicted-rule mean is barely above raw unaligned foreign transfer and barely above the random controls, while still well below the post hoc upper bound. At $f=5.0$, the predicted rule is marginally above random but far below the post hoc upper bound. Most of the gap therefore reflects pair-specific selection rather than a convention recoverable by these simple polarity rules.

## Sender-encoding decomposition {#app:sender-encoding}

This section supports the threshold-free sender-encoding scatter in Figure \ref{fig-encoding-scatter}. The traces record each sender's intended action directly, so the action-linked effect uses intended cooperation/defection rather than an executed-action fallback. The regime-linked effect uses the same coarse split as the analysis code, $\hat f < 3.5$ versus $\hat f \ge 3.5$. For the sensitivity check below, a sender-seed pair is labeled \emph{mixed} if both the regime-linked and action-linked mean absolute effects clear threshold $\tau$, \emph{regime-leaning} if only the regime effect clears it, \emph{action-leaning} if only the action effect clears it, and \emph{weak or unclear} otherwise.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
```
```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from collections import defaultdict
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm

sender_ids = sorted(set(row["sender_id"] for row in SENDER_CAUSAL_MATRIX_ROWS))
receiver_ids = sorted(set(row["receiver_id"] for row in SENDER_CAUSAL_MATRIX_ROWS))
f_panels = [("3.5", r"$f=3.5$"), ("5.0", r"$f=5.0$")]

pair_signed = defaultdict(list)
for row in SENDER_CAUSAL_MATRIX_ROWS:
    key = (row["true_f"], row["sender_id"], row["receiver_id"])
    pair_signed[key].append(float(row["delta_p_cooperate_1_minus_0"]) * 100.0)

signed_panels = []
for f_value, _ in f_panels:
    panel = []
    for sender_id in sender_ids:
        row_values = []
        for receiver_id in receiver_ids:
            vals = pair_signed[(f_value, sender_id, receiver_id)]
            row_values.append(sum(vals) / len(vals))
        panel.append(row_values)
    signed_panels.append(panel)

signed_vmax = max(abs(value) for panel in signed_panels for row in panel for value in row)
signed_norm = TwoSlopeNorm(vmin=-signed_vmax, vcenter=0.0, vmax=signed_vmax)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.6, 2.25), constrained_layout=True)
for idx, (ax, panel, (_, title)) in enumerate(zip(axes, signed_panels, f_panels)):
    im = ax.imshow(panel, cmap="RdBu_r", norm=signed_norm)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(receiver_ids)))
    ax.set_xticklabels([rid.replace("agent_", "A") for rid in receiver_ids], fontsize=8)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(sender_ids)))
    ax.set_yticklabels([sid.replace("agent_", "A") for sid in sender_ids], fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xlabel("Receiver")
    if idx == 0:
        ax.set_ylabel("Sender")
    for i in range(len(sender_ids)):
        for j in range(len(receiver_ids)):
            color = "white" if abs(panel[i][j]) > 0.55 * signed_vmax else "black"
            ax.text(j, i, f"{panel[i][j]:+.1f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5, color=color)
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((i - 0.5, i - 0.5), 1, 1, fill=False, edgecolor="black", linewidth=1.0))

cbar = fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes.ravel().tolist(), shrink=0.88)
cbar.set_label(r"Mean $\Delta P(C)$ (pp)", fontsize=8)
cbar.ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)

signed_sender_fig_path = GENERATED_FIG_ROOT / "fig-sender-probe-signed.pdf"
fig.savefig(signed_sender_fig_path, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)
print(
    render_figure_here(
        "fig-sender-probe-signed",
        r"Cross-seed cancellation of signed sender-probe effects. Each heatmap cell shows the signed mean change in receiver cooperation when forcing one sender's token to 1 rather than 0, averaged across 15 seeds. Because sender polarities differ across seeds, positive and negative effects can cancel; small signed means therefore indicate direction instability, not absence of within-seed receiver influence. Figure \ref{fig-endpoint-panels} shows absolute effect magnitudes.",
        signed_sender_fig_path,
        width=r"0.76\linewidth",
        position="H",
    )
)
```

# Observation-noise sweep {#app:noise}

The noise sweep tests whether the communication advantage changes when private signal quality varies at evaluation time. Agents were trained at $\sigma = 0.5$; we evaluate at $\sigma \in \{0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0\}$. Table \ref{tbl-noise} reports the $f=5.0$ panel; the gap pattern at $f=3.5$ is also non-monotone in $\sigma$ and does not follow the same shape across the sweep.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(
    render_table_here(
        "tbl-noise",
        r"Communication retains a large advantage across the full evaluation-time noise sweep, and the gap is larger under the noisiest observations than under perfect information. Cooperation rates at $f=5.0$ under varying evaluation-time noise $\sigma$ (agents were trained at $\sigma=0.5$). The non-monotone middle rows show that this is an endpoint sensitivity check rather than a calibrated psychometric curve, but the larger gap at $\sigma=1.0$ than at $\sigma=0$ is still consistent with messages carrying regime-relevant information when private signals are less reliable.",
        render_noise_table(),
    )
)
```

This sweep changes observation noise only at evaluation time. It should therefore be read as endpoint sensitivity rather than evidence about how communication would develop if agents were trained under different noise levels.

### Design note {#app:msgsource-provenance}

The message-source comparison is only interpretable when the receiver interface and training objective are held fixed. Comparisons that change both the message source and other training details would make the mechanism harder to identify. We therefore base the main interpretation on contrasts within the matched message-source design.

# Reproducibility details {#app:repro}

The reported training runs use independent PPO with 4 agents, horizon $T=100$, 8 parallel environments counted in environment episodes, two 64-unit hidden layers, learning rate $3\times 10^{-4}$, $\gamma=0.99$, $\lambda=0.95$, clip ratio $0.2$, value-loss coefficient $0.5$, max-grad-norm $0.5$, and reward scaling by 20.0. Communication runs use a binary vocabulary, 4 sender slots, message dropout 0.1, linear action-entropy annealing from 0.01 to 0.001, linear message-entropy annealing from 0.01 to 0, and no positive-signalling or listening auxiliary losses.

Across experiments, the environment uses endowment 4.0, multiplier set $\{0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 5.0\}$, private-noise standard deviations $(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5)$, regime persistence $\rho=0.05$, and tremble probability 0.05. Main claims are based on 15 training seeds per condition with checkpoints at 25k, 50k, 100k, and 150k episodes; reported evaluation summaries are greedy means over those 15 seeds unless a table or caption says otherwise. The software stack targets Python 3.10 with PyTorch 2.10.0 and PettingZoo 1.18.1.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

import re

COMPUTE_BATCH_LOGS = {
    "comm_full_clean_learned": HETZNER_RESULTS_ROOT
    / "phase3_vecstraight_clean_msgsource_learned_15seeds_hetzner_20260410/status/progress.log",
    "comm_reduced_zeroaux": ZEROAUX_COMM_REDUCED_ROOT
    / "status/progress.log",
    "nocomm_full_canonical": HETZNER_RESULTS_ROOT
    / "phase3_vecstraight_comm_history_factorial_without_comm_full_history_15seeds_hetzner_20260330par24/status/progress.log",
    "nocomm_reduced_canonical": HETZNER_RESULTS_ROOT
    / "phase3_vecstraight_comm_history_factorial_without_comm_reduced_history_15seeds_hetzner_20260330par24/status/progress.log",
    "clean_uniform": HETZNER_RESULTS_ROOT
    / "phase3_vecstraight_clean_msgsource_uniform_15seeds_hetzner_20260410/status/progress.log",
    "clean_public_random": HETZNER_RESULTS_ROOT
    / "phase3_vecstraight_clean_msgsource_public_random_15seeds_hetzner_20260410/status/progress.log",
    "clean_fixed0": HETZNER_RESULTS_ROOT
    / "phase3_vecstraight_clean_msgsource_fixed0_15seeds_hetzner_20260410/status/progress.log",
    "clean_fixed1": HETZNER_RESULTS_ROOT
    / "phase3_vecstraight_clean_msgsource_fixed1_15seeds_hetzner_20260410/status/progress.log",
}


def progress_batch_stats(path):
    lines = Path(path).read_text().splitlines()
    ts_re = re.compile(r"^\[(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2})\]")
    train_start = train_end = None
    max_parallel = None
    for line in lines:
        if "train batch start" in line or "batch start" in line:
            match = ts_re.match(line)
            if match:
                train_start = datetime.strptime(match.group(1), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
            mp = re.search(r"max_parallel=(\d+)", line)
            if mp:
                max_parallel = int(mp.group(1))
        elif "train batch done" in line or "batch done" in line:
            match = ts_re.match(line)
            if match:
                train_end = datetime.strptime(match.group(1), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
    if train_start is None or train_end is None or max_parallel is None:
        raise ValueError(f"incomplete batch log: {path}")
    batch_hours = (train_end - train_start).total_seconds() / 3600.0
    active_seed_processes = min(max_parallel, 15)
    seed_hours = batch_hours if active_seed_processes >= 15 else batch_hours * active_seed_processes / 15.0
    worker_hours = batch_hours * active_seed_processes
    return {
        "batch_hours": batch_hours,
        "seed_hours": seed_hours,
        "worker_hours": worker_hours,
        "active_seed_processes": active_seed_processes,
        "max_parallel": max_parallel,
    }


compute_stats = {name: progress_batch_stats(path) for name, path in COMPUTE_BATCH_LOGS.items()}
clean_names = ("comm_full_clean_learned", "clean_uniform", "clean_public_random", "clean_fixed0", "clean_fixed1")
factorial_names = (
    "comm_full_clean_learned",
    "comm_reduced_zeroaux",
    "nocomm_full_canonical",
    "nocomm_reduced_canonical",
)
clean_batch_hours = [compute_stats[name]["batch_hours"] for name in clean_names]
factorial_batch_hours = [compute_stats[name]["batch_hours"] for name in factorial_names]
factorial_seed_hours = [compute_stats[name]["seed_hours"] for name in factorial_names]
timed_worker_hours = sum(stats["worker_hours"] for stats in compute_stats.values())

print(
    f"Approximate wall-clock from batch logs is as follows. The full-history learned-communication arm uses the clean zero-aux message-source run and took about {fmt_num(compute_stats['comm_full_clean_learned']['batch_hours'], 1)} h with {compute_stats['comm_full_clean_learned']['active_seed_processes']} active seed processes. The zero-aux reduced-history communication arm took about {fmt_num(compute_stats['comm_reduced_zeroaux']['batch_hours'], 1)} h with {compute_stats['comm_reduced_zeroaux']['active_seed_processes']} active seed processes. The canonical full- and reduced-history no-communication baselines took {fmt_num(compute_stats['nocomm_full_canonical']['batch_hours'], 1)} h and {fmt_num(compute_stats['nocomm_reduced_canonical']['batch_hours'], 1)} h, respectively, with {compute_stats['nocomm_full_canonical']['active_seed_processes']} active seed processes. The matched message-source controls used 15 active seed processes; 15-seed training batches took {fmt_num(min(clean_batch_hours), 1)}--{fmt_num(max(clean_batch_hours), 1)} h depending on mode. Across the unique timed batches, these reported training runs account for about {fmt_num(timed_worker_hours, 0)} seed-worker-hours. The no-communication baselines have no message channel, so communication-specific shaping terms are inactive for those arms."
)
```

These figures are approximate wall-clock disclosures from batch logs rather than exact CPU-core accounting. The logs record parallelism but not per-job peak memory, so the compute disclosure should be read as approximate rather than exhaustive.

# Broader impacts {#app:broader}

This paper is a methodological study of emergent communication in a stylized social dilemma, so its most direct positive impact is scientific: it offers sharper tests for distinguishing robust communication from simpler shared-cue effects, and it highlights evaluation failures that can mislead multi-agent reinforcement-learning research. Better diagnosis of when messages are actually portable could improve how coordination systems are benchmarked and compared.

Possible negative impacts are indirect but real. Techniques that make agent coordination more effective or make message channels easier to exploit could be adapted in larger strategic multi-agent systems, including settings where strong coordination is undesirable. A more immediate risk is scientific overclaiming: if brittle, population-specific conventions are mistaken for portable shared protocols, researchers may deploy or interpret learned communication systems with more confidence than the evidence supports.
